clue.text: Is this helmet made of cotton?

definitions.text: Is this helmet made of cotton?

parts.words: Is this helmet made of cotton?
parts.note: a motorcyclist's protective headgear shares its first word with a coarse cotton or linen fabric used for towels, so the question asks whether that helmet is woven from it

explanation.surface: Someone innocently asks what a motorcyclist's protective helmet is made from.
explanation.walkthrough: Crash is a coarse plain-weave fabric of cotton or linen, so the clue jokes that a crash helmet might be made of it.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the kind of protective helmet worn by riders and a rough cloth woven from cotton or linen.

clue.text: Stone needing medical treatment (Holmes's was blue)

definitions.meaning: a red gemstone, especially a garnet cut in a rounded shape
a painful boil or cluster of boils under the skin that a doctor must deal with

explanation.surface: A gem, a medical complaint, and a nod to a Sherlock Holmes story about a blue jewel.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed aside recalls Conan Doyle's story 'The Adventure of the Blue Carbuncle', confirming the gem sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a garnet gemstone cut en cabochon and a severe skin abscess, two unrelated senses.

clue.text: Trouble with gnats causing anxiety

indicators.note: to trouble something is to disturb it, so the letters of the insects are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: Being pestered by gnats makes someone anxious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trouble' shuffles the letters of GNATS.
explanation.definitionFit: Angst is a German loan word for deep dread or existential worry.

clue.text: The 20'ac guards his fellow-countrymen

parts.note: the papal guard in Rome is drawn from one Alpine nation, so its members' compatriots are people of that nation, named by its Latin name

explanation.surface: The guards of the papal state protect their own countrymen.
explanation.walkthrough: 20 across is the Vatican, whose guard is the Swiss Guard; Helvetia is the Latin name of Switzerland.
explanation.definitionFit: Helvetian means Swiss, and the Vatican's guards are recruited from Switzerland.

clue.text: Impair social standing, being without one bit of jewellery

parts.note: to mar something is to spoil or impair it

indicators.note: a word being without another here means it stands outside it, wrapping it

parts.note: caste is a hereditary rank in society
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone loses social status by not having a single piece of jewellery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being without' is a containment, not a lack: I goes inside CASTE.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcasite is iron pyrites cut and polished to glitter in brooches and rings.

clue.text: Island stomach upset (subject to variation)

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset turns the pair of words upside down, so the whole run is read backwards

parts.note: Elba is the Mediterranean island of Napoleon's exile
tum is an informal word for the stomach

explanation.surface: Someone's stomach gets upset on an island, a changeable condition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' reverses ELBA and TUM together, giving MUT then ABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something mutable is changeable, liable to alter over time.

clue.text: Russian wife of Boaz in Cornwall

parts.note: red stands for a Russian, from the colour of Soviet communism
in the Bible, Ruth the Moabite married Boaz

explanation.surface: A Russian woman married to the biblical Boaz lives in Cornwall.
explanation.walkthrough: Redruth is a town in Cornwall, the county at England's south-western tip.
explanation.definitionFit: Redruth is an old mining town in the far south-west of England, so it is a place found there.

clue.text: All going thus to Widdicombe Fair?

definitions.text: All going thus to Widdicombe Fair?

parts.words: All going thus to Widdicombe Fair?
parts.note: the Devon folk song about Uncle Tom Cobley and his companions riding to the fair has a refrain beginning 'all ...', here hinted at

explanation.surface: Everyone is heading off to a Devon country fair.
explanation.walkthrough: The folk song 'Widecombe Fair' has the refrain 'All along, down along, out along lee', so 'all' goes this way.
explanation.definitionFit: In the song's refrain the companions travel 'all along', the adverb that follows the word all.

clue.text: Not good for a stretch in 13 anyway

indicators.note: anyway suggests the letters may go in any way at all, so they are rearranged

parts.note: 13 across is the old Spanish kingdom, Castile

explanation.surface: Something won't stretch while in the old Spanish region, whatever happens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyway' rearranges IN plus CASTILE, the answer to 13 across.
explanation.definitionFit: A material that cannot be pulled out and spring back lacks elasticity.

clue.text: Note dubious type of community spirit

parts.note: E is a musical note
a doubting Thomas is a sceptic, and Thos is the short form of Thomas

explanation.surface: Someone observes a suspicious character who resembles a spirit of togetherness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dubious type' refers to doubting Thomas, the sceptical apostle, abbreviated in the old way as Thos.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethos is the characteristic spirit and beliefs of a group or community.

clue.text: Controlled reorganization of glue trade

indicators.note: a reorganization rearranges what is there, so the letters of the two words are put into new order

explanation.surface: The glue business was reorganized under strict control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reorganization of' shuffles GLUE and TRADE together.
explanation.definitionFit: Regulated means governed or kept in check by rules.

clue.text: Witchcraft brings honour to a Haitian leader

parts.note: the OBE, Officer of the Order of the British Empire, is a British honour

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter, here of Haitian

explanation.surface: Sorcery earns a Haitian leader an award.
explanation.walkthrough: Obeah is a form of folk magic practised in the Caribbean.
explanation.definitionFit: Obeah is a system of sorcery and spells from West African tradition practised in the West Indies.

clue.text: Join, but turn it thus to release

indicators.note: turn tells us to reverse the two letters of the word it within the synonym

parts.note: to unite is to join together

explanation.surface: Someone joins things but, turning them a certain way, frees them.
explanation.walkthrough: In UNITE the letters IT are turned round to TI, and 'thus' points to the result.
explanation.definitionFit: To untie a knot or bond is to loosen it and set free what it held.

clue.text: Kentucky diet for the unhappy Greek moke?

parts.note: blue means sad or unhappy
moke is British slang for a donkey

explanation.surface: Someone asks what a gloomy Greek donkey might eat in Kentucky.
explanation.walkthrough: Kentucky is the Bluegrass State; 'diet for the' links the definition to the wordplay, with a hint at grass as fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Kentucky is nicknamed the Bluegrass State after the meadow grass that grows there.

clue.text: I entered an English home here in old Spain

indicators.note: a letter that has entered a word goes inside it

parts.note: the saying is that an Englishman's home is his castle

explanation.surface: A traveller enters an English house while in old Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entered' puts I inside CASTLE, from the saying that an Englishman's home is his castle.
explanation.definitionFit: Castile was a medieval kingdom at the heart of what became Spain.

clue.text: Plant is a money-maker headed by the male side…

indicators.note: in a down clue, a word headed by another has that other placed above it, first

parts.note: the spear side is the male line of a family, as opposed to the distaff side
the Mint is where coins are made

explanation.surface: A money-making enterprise is led by the men of the family.
explanation.walkthrough: The spear side is an old term for male descent, matched by the distaff side in the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Spearmint is a common garden herb of the mint family.

clue.text: One who hates accepting manuscript, the little beast

indicators.note: a word accepting another takes it inside itself

parts.note: a hater is a person who hates

explanation.surface: A grumpy critic takes in a manuscript about a small animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One who hates' looks like a character in the scene but simply gives a word for a person who hates; the little beast is a pet rodent.
explanation.definitionFit: A hamster is a small burrowing rodent often kept as a pet.

clue.text: … this boss (on the other) creates one art form in a month

indicators.note: the shuffled letters go in the month's name, inside it

parts.note: March is a month

indicators.note: to form something is to shape it, so the letters are put into a new arrangement

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A female boss creates an artwork within a month, following the previous clue.
explanation.walkthrough: '(on the other)' means on the other side, the distaff side, against the spear side of 14 down. 'form' rearranges I and ART to TRIA, which goes 'in' MARCH.
explanation.definitionFit: A matriarch is a woman who heads a family, the female counterpart of a patriarch.

clue.text: Christopher, out West, on a trail that's enjoying a revival

indicators.note: out says the letter for West is removed from the name

parts.note: Sir Christopher Wren was the architect of St Paul's Cathedral
a scent is the trail an animal leaves for hounds to follow

explanation.surface: An explorer called Christopher heads west on a trail that is reviving.
explanation.walkthrough: Christopher Wren loses his W to leave REN, then comes A and SCENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Renascent means being reborn or coming back into being after decline.

clue.text: One earl created by English queen from 13

indicators.note: created signals that the letters are made into something new, rearranged

explanation.surface: An English queen from Spain creates a nobleman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'created' rearranges ONE and EARL; 13 across is Castile, and Eleanor of Castile was the queen of Edward I.
explanation.definitionFit: Eleanor of Castile was a Spanish princess who became consort of Edward I of England.

clue.text: Difficulty over prelate being out of work? Nonsense!

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece over another is written above it, so first

parts.note: the rub is the difficulty, as in Hamlet's 'there's the rub'

indicators.note: being out of something means losing it, so those letters drop away

parts.note: a bishop is a senior churchman, a prelate
op, short for opus, is a work

explanation.surface: A problem arises over a bishop who has lost his job: absurd!
explanation.walkthrough: 'being out of work' reads as unemployment, but it trims OP (opus, a work) from the churchman; 'the rub' for a difficulty comes from Hamlet.
explanation.definitionFit: Rubbish is an exclamation dismissing something as foolish talk.

clue.text: A city almost back in the forefront

definitions.text: A city almost back in the forefront

indicators.note: the reversed letters are placed in the word for the forefront

parts.note: the van, short for vanguard, is the forefront

indicators.note: back says the run of letters is read in reverse
almost cuts the last letter from the word city

explanation.surface: A city nearly falls back to the leading position.
explanation.walkthrough: A plus CIT (city 'almost') read 'back' gives ATIC, which goes 'in' VAN; the whole describes the papal city-state.
explanation.definitionFit: Vatican City is the tiny sovereign city-state in Rome, the centre of the Catholic Church.

clue.text: Energy needed to contain volcano in SE Asia

indicators.note: one word made to contain another holds it inside

parts.note: vim is energy or vigour
Etna is the volcano on Sicily

explanation.surface: Energy is needed to keep a volcano in check in South-East Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Energy' looks like E but here gives the three-letter word for vigour; Etna is the volcano on Sicily.
explanation.definitionFit: Vietnam is a country on the eastern coast of the Indochinese peninsula.

clue.text: Record-holder to do a spiritualistic stunt?

definitions.meaning: the rotating platform on a gramophone that a disc sits on
at seances, mediums made a table appear to tip and spin, read here as two words

explanation.surface: A gramophone part also describes a seance trick.
explanation.walkthrough: Table-turning was a Victorian seance trick; split, the answer is to turn a table.
explanation.definitionFit: The disc platform of a record player shares its name with the phrase for making a seance table move.

clue.text: Rough, we hear, but an excellent fellow

definitions.meaning: rough sounds like ruff, which in card games means to play a ...
an old informal word for a thoroughly good, reliable person

explanation.surface: Someone sounds rough but is really a fine fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: In whist or bridge, to ruff (said like rough) is to trump a trick; a trump was also old slang for a good sort.
explanation.definitionFit: To ruff in cards is to beat a trick with a trump, and a trump is also an old term for a splendid person.

clue.text: Course for a singer

definitions.meaning: the general drift or course of something
a male voice pitched above baritone

explanation.surface: A course of study for a vocalist.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'course' sense is the settled way something proceeds.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both the general drift of events and a high male voice.

clue.text: Old Indian rulers — who used writing fluid we hear?

indicators.note: we hear signals that the word is said aloud, matching another in sound

parts.note: inkers are people who apply ink

explanation.surface: Ancient South American lords are said to have written with ink.
explanation.walkthrough: Said in a non-rhotic British accent, INKERS sounds like INCAS.
explanation.definitionFit: The Incas were the ruling people of an Andean empire before the Spanish conquest.

clue.text: Watercourse where water became wine on third of July

parts.note: Cana in Galilee is where, in John's Gospel, Jesus turned water into wine

indicators.note: the third of a word is its third letter, here of July

explanation.surface: A stream where a biblical miracle happened in early summer.
explanation.walkthrough: CANA plus L, the third letter of July.
explanation.definitionFit: A canal is an artificial waterway built for boats or irrigation.

clue.text: Rugby-style marriage

definitions.meaning: rugby ... is the fifteen-a-side code of rugby football
a joining of two people in wedlock

explanation.surface: A wedding conducted in the manner of a rugby match.
explanation.walkthrough: Rugby comes in two codes, union and league.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names one code of rugby and also a wedding or joining together.

clue.text: Johnson's reason for defining "pastern" as "horse's knee"

definitions.text: Johnson's reason for defining "pastern" as "horse's knee"

parts.words: Johnson's reason for defining "pastern" as "horse's knee"
parts.note: Dr Johnson's dictionary got the part of a horse's leg wrong, and when a lady asked why he simply blamed his own lack of knowledge

explanation.surface: Why did Dr Johnson's dictionary misdefine part of a horse's leg?
explanation.walkthrough: Asked why he did it, Johnson famously replied 'Ignorance, madam, pure ignorance.' The pastern is actually the part of the foot between fetlock and hoof.
explanation.definitionFit: Johnson confessed to simply not knowing, a lack of knowledge.

clue.text: Boy's got some meat in this material

parts.note: Peter's: the possessive of the boy's name Peter
ham is cured meat

explanation.surface: A boy has some meat wrapped in this fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: Petersham is a thick corded ribbon or heavy woollen cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Petersham is a stiff ribbed ribbon used for hatbands and waistbands, or a heavy overcoat cloth.

clue.text: He had a great deal to drink for example in Sparta

definitions.text: He had a great deal to drink for example in Sparta

parts.note: taken as written
a lot is a great deal

explanation.surface: A man drank heavily, setting an example in ancient Sparta.
explanation.walkthrough: Spartans made their serfs drunk to show their sons the evils of drink, so the whole clue describes one.
explanation.definitionFit: A helot was a state serf of ancient Sparta, sometimes forced to get drunk as a warning to youth.
